work.text: One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, or Tsuki no Hyakushi (月百姿) in Japanese, is a collection of 100 ōban-size ukiyo-e woodblock prints by Japanese artist Tsukioka Yoshitoshi printed in batches, starting in 1885 until 1892.

source.author: Wikipedia contributors
source.title: One Hundred Aspects of the Moon

work.text: Yoshitoshi's most celebrated work is his series entitled Tsuki Hiak'ushi ("The Hundred Moons"), which occupied him over five years to complete.

source.author: Basil Stewart
source.title: Japanese Colour-Prints and the Subjects They Illustrate
source.publisher: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner (Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: The subjects are drawn from various sources in Japanese and Chinese history and literature, Kabuki and Noh theatre, and even contemporary Edo (modern Tokyo), linked only by the presence of the Moon in each print.

source.author: Wikipedia contributors
source.title: One Hundred Aspects of the Moon

moment.text: This was the most successful and still the most famous of Yoshitoshi's print series. People would queue before dawn to buy each new design and still find the edition sold out.

source.author: Wikipedia contributors
source.title: One Hundred Aspects of the Moon

matters.text: Nobunaga's young retainer Kinoshita Tōkichirō (later known as Toyotomi Hideyoshi) played an important role in attaining the victory at Inabayama.
Horio Yoshiharu then guided Kinoshita Hideyoshi and the small assault force around to the back of the mountain, where they climbed the steep slopes by the light of a full moon.
